Recent work supports attribute-specific text representations and alignment with collaborative signals, but the strongest matches generally require pretrained language models. [MARS (CIKM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) uses attribute-aware text encoding and attribute-wise user–item matching to distinguish multiple preferences. [CLA-Rec (ICDM 2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884256/) contrastively aligns LLM-derived description embeddings with collaborative representations, explicitly addressing their semantic gap. [HSTU-BLaIR (2025)](https://kdd2025llm4ecommerce.github.io/assets/accepted/13_HSTU_BLaIR_Lightweight_Cont.pdf) projects and fuses text and ID embeddings and introduces text-aware negative sampling; its text features come from a pretrained, review-based BLaIR checkpoint, making that implementation unsuitable here. These papers provide design ideas, not evidence that a scratch-trained lightweight encoder will deliver equivalent gains.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis is a randomly initialized token embedding table with masked mean pooling or a small text CNN over permitted titles/descriptions, jointly trained with item IDs inside one NextItNet network. Fuse projected text features through a learned gate, retain causal dilated convolutions, and score candidates through the same learned item representation. A small auxiliary ID–text contrastive loss could encourage item-specific distinctions while next-item prediction determines relevance; this is a proposed adaptation, not a verified result from the cited papers. Text overlap should not automatically define positive item pairs: similar descriptions can describe substitutes, incompatible variants, or unrelated current intent. Compare against the corrected ID-only baseline using the fixed macro validation HR@10, with one trained checkpoint per category.
